## Setup

As before we will use materials from @maindonald in this case excerpts from Chapter 6. I'm incorporating some excerpts from @jamesbook.

Consider that we have an experiment with covariate(s) $X$ and response $Y$ with either two possibilities *yes* or *no*. For convenience, we use the binary codes for the response variable, say 1 for yes and 0 for no. We use **logistic regression** to model the probability that $Y$ is 1 or 0.

We use the following notation to denote the probability of having a *yes* given that the value of $X=x$.

$$      
p(X=x)= Pr(Y=1 | X=x)
$$

Thus, if $p(X=x)>0.5$ we can say that $X=x$ belongs to the class 1. Our first attempt may be to use linear regression as follows:

$$
    p(X)= \theta_0+ \theta_1 X
$$

However, when we use such a model we may encounter negative probabilities as the following book-example shows.

![](Figures/fig_logreg.png)

We apply the so-called **logistic function**

$$      p(X)= \frac{\exp(\theta_0+ \theta_1 X)}{1+ \exp(\theta_0+\theta_1 X)} $$\

```{r,echo=TRUE}
library(sigmoid)
library(ggplot2)
input = seq(-10,10,by=.05)
df = data.frame(input,logistic(input))
q<-ggplot(df,aes(input,logistic(input)))+geom_line()
q
```

After some algebraic manipulation, we can show that

$$
\log \left( \frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)} \right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 X
$$

The left-hand of the previous expression is called the **log-odds** or **logit**.

> There is an *ad hoc* use of the logistic regression for prediction. For instance for a cut-off value of $0.5$ in the logistic regression model we use $\hat{p}(X)$ as follows

$$
    \hat{Y}=
    \begin{cases}
        0 & \textrm{if } \hat{p}(X)  \le 0.5 \\
        1 &  \textrm{if } \hat{p}(X) > 0.5
    \end{cases}
$$

> However, this use is problematic at best. Since we will need some scientific justification of the choice of the cut-off.

Whereas we can use our data to estimate the coefficients $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ using a least squares approach, this is not normally used. Instead the method of **maximum likelihood** is preferred.

The likelihood is the joint probability of the observed data values, given the model parameters. The so-called **deviance** is minus twice the logarithm of the likelihood. Thus, maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the deviance.

The likelihood function is defined by

$$      
\ell (\theta_0,\theta_1)= \prod_{i:y_i=0} p(x_i) \prod_{i':y_i'=1} (1-p(x_{i'}))
$$

Some calculus is required to find out the estimates $\hat{\theta}_0$ and $\hat{\theta}_1$ that **maximize** this likelihood function.

> The role of minimizing the deviance plays a very similar role to minimizing sum of squares in regression.

```{r}
library(ISLR)
attach(Default)

default.logit<-glm(default ~ balance, family=binomial(link = "logit"))
anova(default.logit)

```

Then, we can find some more useful information using the *summary* function

```{r}
summary(default.logit)
```

As with multiple linear regression, we can expand the model to accommodate more predictors $$      
\log \left( \frac{p(X)}{1-p(X)} \right) = \theta_0 + \theta_1 X_1 + \cdots+ \theta_p X_p,
$$

where $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ are $p$ predictors. And the corresponding logistic function is given by

$$      p(X)= \frac{\exp(\theta_0 + \theta_1 X_1 + \cdots+ \theta_p X_p)}{1 +exp(\theta_0 + \theta_1 X_1 + \cdots+ \theta_p X_p) }
    $$

### Example of EDA and analysis of multivariate logistic model

A book example (from @maindonald) about Southern Corroboree frog. The variables are

- pres.abs whether the frogs were found

- easting reference point

- northing reference point

- altitude

- distance to neareast extant population

- NoOfPools number of potential breeding pools

- NoOfSites number of potential breeding sites

- avran mean rainfall for Spring period

- meanmin mean minimum Spring temperature

```{r}
library(DAAG)
attach(frogs)
```

A quick look at the distribution of those variables

```{r}
pairs(frogs[,4:10],oma=c(2,2,2,2),cex=0.5)
```

This example is interesting because we can play with different transformations on this data set

- We have some skewed variables (e.g., distance, NoOfPools, NoOfSites) for which a logarithmic transformation may be useful

- Two of these variables are counts, those a square-root transformation may be also useful.

Let's consider in practice how can we perform these changes when exploring our models

```{r}
# a handy function to plot changes in our variables
par(mfrow=c(2,3))
for(nam in c("distance", "NoOfPools")){
  y<-frogs[,nam]
  plot(density(y), main="",xlab=nam)
  plot(density(log(y)),main="",xlab=paste0("log ",nam))
  plot(density(sqrt(y)),main="",xlab=paste0("sqrt ",nam))
}
```

#### A simplified model

Let's consider this model

```{r}
frogs.glm0 <- glm(pres.abs ~ altitude + log(distance)+
                  log(NoOfPools)+NoOfSites+avrain+meanmin+
                  meanmax,family=binomial, data=frogs)
summary(frogs.glm0)
```

In the text, there is an explanation of why we should take the $p$-values cautiously based on the nature of the experiment. A simplified model proposed was

```{r}
frogs.glm <- glm(formula = pres.abs ~ log(distance)+
                   log(NoOfPools)+ meanmin+ meanmax,
                 family=binomial,data=frogs)
summary(frogs.glm)
```

Note that the deviance was not changed and the variable *meanmax* is now with a small $p$-value.

#### Some exploratory analysis

To see how each of these variables changes when the other variables are held at their mean values.

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(1,4),pty="s")
termplot(frogs.glm,data=frogs)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

> Displaying the residuals does not add insights into the model. In general, they are very hard to interpret.

```         
```

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(1,4))
plot(frogs.glm,panel=panel.smooth)
```

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(1,4))
termplot(frogs.glm,data=frogs,partial.resid=TRUE)
```

An alternative to check predictive accuracy is to use cross-validation. The accuracy of the model is stored in the element *acc.cv* of the function CVbinary.

```{r}
for (j in 1:4){
  randsam<-sample(1:10,212,replace=TRUE)
  all.acc <-CVbinary(frogs.glm0,rand=randsam)$acc.cv
  reduced.acc<-CVbinary(frogs.glm,rand=randsam)$acc.cv
  cat("\nAll variables",round(all.acc,3)," Reduced model",round(reduced.acc,3),"\n=====\n")
}

```
